text:
Droit de la famille — 21827

2021 QCCS 1881

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

TERREBONNE

No.:

700-12-051546-208

700-04-031260-208

DATE:

May 13
, 2021

_____________________________________________________________________

BY

THE HONOURABLE

PETER KALICHMAN, J.S.C.

_____________________________________________________________________

M. S.

Plaintiff

v.

Y. K.

Defendant

_____________________________________________________________________

rectified
JUDGMENT

application
to dismiss based on s. 21.1 of the divorce act

_____________________________________________________________________

OVERVIEW

[
1
]

M. S. (the
Wife
) asks the Court to
dismiss all the proceedings filed by her husband, Y. K. (the
Husband
),
in the context of their ongoing divorce. The Wife’s application is based on
section
21.1
of the
Divorce Act
[1]

(the
Act
), which provides the courts with discretionary power to dismiss
or to strike out any proceeding filed by a spouse who refuses to remove a
barrier
to religious remarriage.

[
2
]

The Husband opposes the application. He claims to have
genuine grounds of a religious nature for refusing to remove the barrier to the
Wife’s remarriage and argues that the Court should therefore refuse to dismiss
his proceedings.

CONTEXT

[
3
]

The parties, who are both observant Jews, were
married in 2006 and have four children.

[
4
]

In May of 2020, after the couple separated, the
Husband instituted proceedings in file number 700-04-031260-208, asking that he
be granted interim access rights to the children and a portion of all child
care benefits (the
04 file
).

[
5
]

Later that same month, the Wife instituted
proceedings in file number 700-12-051546-208, seeking a divorce (the
Divorce
file
). The divorce will not put an end to the marriage from a religious
perspective. For that, the Wife requires a bill of Jewish divorcement, or a
get
,
which the Husband must agree to give her. On the basis of a husband’s agreement
to give the
get
and a wife’s consent to receive it, the
get
is
pronounced by a religious tribunal known as a
beth din
.

[
6
]

Without the
get
, the Wife cannot remarry
in accordance with her faith. She has been asking the Husband to give her the
get

since before the proceedings were brought in the Divorce file.

[
7
]

On September 14, 2020, the Wife served the
Husband with an affidavit in accordance with
s. 21.1 (2)
the
Act
, calling upon
him to remove the barrier to her remarriage by agreeing to give her the
get
.

[
8
]

The Husband did not immediately answer the
affidavit and, as a result, in October 2020, the Wife brought the present
application to dismiss the Husband’s proceedings, to foreclose the Husband from
pleading or filing any additional proceedings and to authorize her to obtain
judgment on an
ex parte
basis (the
Application
). The conclusions
of the Application are directed at both the Divorce file and the 04 file.

[
9
]

On April 12, 2021, the Husband filed an
affidavit, or sworn declaration, in accordance with
s. 21.1 (3)
of the
Act
, to
contest the Application.
[2]
The Husband’s position is summarized below:

a.

He acknowledges that he is unwilling to give the
Wife a
get
at this time;

b.

He affirms that to be valid, the
get
must
be given freely, without any pressure or constraints;

c.

So long as a conflictual situation exists
between them, he cannot in good conscience and in accordance with religious
rules, give the
get
to the Wife and no
get
given in such
circumstances would be valid;

d.

There is no urgency for him to give the
get

at this time because the Wife has not even received a civil divorce and cannot,
therefore, remarry. The Application is thus premature;

e.

He was and remains willing to proceed before a
beth
din
in the State of New York;

f.

He is entitled to file proceedings to defend himself
in the Divorce file and should not be prevented from doing so; and

g.

He is willing to reach an amicable resolution of
all issues between him and the Wife, including by mediation or judicial
settlement conference.

[
10
]

According to the Wife, the Husband’s refusal to
give the
get
is not based on religious reasons but is rather a pretext
to extract concessions from her in the context of the Divorce file.

SECTION 21.1 OF THE ACT

[
11
]

The
Act
was amended in 1990 to add
section 21.1
.
While it makes no reference to any religious group in particular, it is clear
that Parliament had in mind the unique challenge faced by an observant Jew
whose spouse refuses to give the
get
. This challenge was described by
Justice Abella in the Supreme Court’s decision in
Bruker v. Marcovitz
.
[3]

[3]
A get is
a Jewish divorce. Only a husband can give one. A wife cannot obtain a get
unless her husband agrees to give it. Under Jewish law, he does so by
“releasing” his wife from the marriage and authorizing her to remarry. The
process takes place before three rabbis in what is known as a beth din, or
rabbinical court.

[4]
The husband must voluntarily give the get and the wife
consent to receive it. When he does not, she is without religious recourse,
retaining the status of his wife and unable to remarry until he decides, in his
absolute discretion, to divorce her. She is known as an agunah or “chained
wife”. Any children she would have on civil remarriage would be considered
“illegitimate” under Jewish law.

[5]
For an observant Jewish woman in Canada, this presents
a dichotomous scenario: under Canadian law, she is free to divorce her husband
regardless of his consent; under Jewish law, however, she remains married to
him unless he gives his consent. This means that while she can remarry under
Canadian law, she is prevented from remarrying in accordance with her religion.
The inability to do so, for many Jewish women, results in the loss of their
ability to remarry at all.

[6]
The vast majority of Jewish husbands freely give their
wives a get. Those who do not, however, represent a long-standing source of
concern and frustration in Jewish communities (…)

[
12
]

In addressing Parliament, Justice Minister, Kim
Campbell, outlined the motivation for the amendments to the
Act
:

The purpose of this bill is to
assist Jewish citizens whose spouses are withholding a religious divorce, which
is called a get, in order to obtain concessions in a civil divorce…

. . .

The consequences to women deprived
of a get and loyal to their faith are severe. They may not remarry within their
faith, even though civilly divorced. If they do remarry, children from a second
civil marriage are considered illegitimate and restricted from practising their
religion. Such consequences to a religious person leave them open to blackmail
from the spouse withholding the get. For example, the spouse could say,
“Give up your claim for support or custody of the children and I will offer the
get.” Even those not contemplating a second marriage find it uncomfortable to
be considered married within their religion to someone they have divorced
civilly.
[4]

[
13
]

While Parliament has no power to grant or to
refuse a religious divorce, it can indirectly address the inequities that may
result from a spouse’s refusal to remove barriers to religious remarriage. This
is precisely what
s. 21.1
of the
Act
purports to do by giving the courts the discretionary
authority to prevent a spouse who refuses to remove such a barrier from seeking
to benefit from the provisions of the Act.

[
14
]

The mechanism set out in
s. 21.1
of the
Act
is triggered
when one spouse serves the other with an affidavit in accordance with
s. 21.1
(2)
. The affidavit confirms that a written request has been made to remove a
barrier to religious remarriage and that, despite the request, the barrier has
not been removed. The spouse who receives the affidavit has fifteen days, or
such other delay as a court may provide, to remove the barrier, failing which
the court can dismiss or strike out any applications or proceedings filed by
that spouse.

[
15
]

Sections 21.1 (2)
and
(3)
of the
Act
, read as
follows:

Affidavit re removal of barriers to
religious remarriage

(2)
In any proceedings under this
Act
, a spouse (in this section
referred to as the “deponent”) may serve on the other spouse and file with the
court an affidavit indicating

(a)
that
the other spouse is the spouse of the deponent;

(b)
the date and place of the
marriage, and the official character of the person who solemnized the marriage;

(c)
the nature of any barriers
to the remarriage of the deponent within the deponent’s religion the removal of
which is within the other spouse’s control;

(d)
where there are any barriers
to the remarriage of the other spouse within the other spouse’s religion the
removal of which is within the deponent’s control, that the deponent

(i)
has removed those barriers, and
the date and circumstances of that removal, or

(ii)
has
signified a willingness to remove those barriers, and the date and
circumstances of that signification;

(e)
that the deponent has, in
writing, requested the other spouse to remove all of the barriers to the
remarriage of the deponent within the deponent’s religion the removal of which
is within the other spouse’s control;

(f)
the
date of the request described in paragraph (e); and

(g)
that the other spouse,
despite the request described in paragraph (e), has failed to remove all of the
barriers referred to in that paragraph.

Powers of court where barriers not
removed

(3)
Where a spouse who has been served with an affidavit under
subsection (2) does not

(a)
within fifteen days after
that affidavit is filed with the court or within such longer period as the
court allows, serve on the deponent and file with the court an affidavit
indicating that all of the barriers referred to in paragraph (2)(e) have been
removed, and

(b)
satisfy the court, in any
additional manner that the court may require, that all of the barriers referred
to in paragraph (2)(e) have been removed, the court may, subject to any terms
that the court considers appropriate,

(c)
dismiss any application
filed by that spouse under this
Act
, and

(d)
strike
out any other pleadings and affidavits filed by that spouse under this
Act
.

[
16
]

Section 21.1 (4)
of the
Act
provides that a
court may refuse to exercise its power to dismiss or strike out proceedings
where the spouse who refuses to remove a barrier to religious remarriage,
demonstrates that the refusal is justified by “genuine grounds of a religious
or conscientious nature”.

(4)
Without limiting the generality of the court’s discretion
under subsection (3), the court may refuse to exercise its powers under
paragraphs (3)(c) and (d) where a spouse who has been served with an affidavit
under subsection (2)

(a)
within fifteen days after
that affidavit is filed with the court or within such longer period as the
court allows, serves on the deponent and files with the court an affidavit
indicating genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for refusing
to remove the barriers referred to in paragraph (2)(e); and

(b)
satisfies the court, in any
additional manner that the court may require, that the spouse has genuine
grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for refusing to remove the
barriers referred to in paragraph (2)(e).

[
17
]

The question of what constitutes “genuine
grounds of a religious or conscientious nature” has been addressed in a number
of decisions rendered by this court, including those referenced below.

[
18
]

In
Droit de la famille
2296, Justice
Tannenbaum, J.S.C., held that consenting to provide the
get
only once a
civil divorce has been pronounced, does not constitute “moral, conscientious or
religious grounds” for refusal.
[5]

[
19
]

In
D.A. c. J.H.
Justice Trahan, J.S.C., ruled
that a spouse’s concern over the manner in which the children would receive
religious education should the other spouse remarry, does not justify the
refusal to give the
get
.
[6]

[
20
]

In
Droit de la famille 3558
, a spouse
argued that the coercive nature of the request under
s. 21.1
of the
Act
, meant
that consent to the
get
could not be freely given and that, as a result,
no rabbinical court would ratify such a divorce. Justice Décarie, J.S.C.
rejected this argument, ruling that the grounds raised by the spouse were
inconsistent with his previous position regarding the
get
and could not
be viewed as a genuine ground of a religious or conscientious nature.
[7]

[
21
]

Finally, in
Droit de la famille – 151954
,
a spouse refused to give the
get
on the basis that religious belief and
conscience required that the couple attempt instead to reconcile. Justice
Mandeville, J.S.C. held that the spouse’s refusal to give the
get
was
not based on a genuine ground of a religous or conscientous nature, particularly
since that same spouse had filed court proceedings that did not seek
reconciliation.
[8]

ANALYSIS

[
22
]

There is no dispute that the Husband has not
agreed to provide the
get
to the Wife. He may be willing to attend a
beth
din
but he knows full well that without his consent, no
get
will be
issued. Consequently, there is clearly a barrier to the Wife’s religious
remarriage that is in the Husband’s sole power to remove.

[
23
]

It is also not disputed that the Wife’s
affidavit of September 14, 2020, conforms to the requirements set out at
s.
21.1(2)
of the
Act
.

[
24
]

With respect to the Husband’s argument regarding
the lack of urgency, the Court does not agree that this is a relevant
consideration. As Justice Mandeville noted in
Droit de la famille – 151954
[9]
, the
Act
contains no such requirement. On the contrary, the fact
that Parliament imposes a 15-day delay in which to reply to the initial
affidavit indicates its intention that the process move quickly, whether or not
the spouse seeking to remove the barrier to religious remarriage has plans to
remarry.

[
25
]

The Court is therefore satisfied that the Wife
has met her burden and that the Court can exercise the powers provided for at
s. 21.1 (3) of the Act and dismiss the Husband’s proceedings. The Court must
now determine whether it should refuse to exercise its power on the basis that
the Husband has a genuine ground of a religious nature to refuse to provide the

get
.

[
26
]

The specific paragraphs of the Husband’s sworn
declaration in which his position is explained are reproduced below:

9. THAT in order for
myself to be able to validly give the Geht to the Plaintiff, it must be done in
a free manner without any pressures or constraints. Moreover, in order for the
Geht to be given, it must be done in a peaceful manner. Therefore as long as
the contested Proceedings are pending before the Courts, I cannot in good and
clear conscience and in accordance with the Religious rules, give the Geht to
the Plaintiff.

16. THAT in response to
allegations contained in paragraphs nine (9) and ten (10), I wish to state that
in accordance with the rules of Orthodox Hassidic Jewish rite, the Geht cannot
be given, due to the high level of conflict and proceedings that are presently
pending before the Courts. Therefore as hereinabove, already mentioned, the
Geht can only be given of a Free Will and in a Peaceful manner and
non-litigious situation.

20. THAT I deny the
response to allegations contained at paragraph seventeen (17), eighteen (18),
nineteen (19) and twenty (20). I reiterate from a deeply Religious and personal
sense of conscience and religious propriety and observance that I cannot give
the Geht to the Plaintiff, given that we are in litigation before the Courts
and the Geht must be given in a free and peaceful manner in order for the Geht
to be valid.

23. THAT as a religious and
devout Orthodox Hassidic Jew, my actions and my decisions are guided by the
traditions and religious rules I have always lived by since birth.

24. THAT it is not
possible for me at this time to freely give a Geht to the Plaintiff, given the
already mentioned litigious and conflictual situation that presently exists
between us.

29. THAT in order for
the Geht to be given, it must be freely given, without any constraints and must
be in a Peaceful situation.

30. THAT until such time
as conflict ceases to exist between the Plaintiff and myself, a Geht cannot be
given and would not be valid.

[
27
]

The Court will first address two letters filed
by the Husband in support of his position.

[
28
]

The first letter is dated March 15, 2021 and is
signed by Rabbi Y. Wosner. Rabbi Wosner sets out certain questions that are
asked of anyone coming before a
beth din
for a
get
and which are
intended to determine if the person is coming of his own free will. At the end
of his letter, Rabbi Wosner adds that his understanding is that the Husband is
thinking of giving the
get
because he is being threatened and is afraid
that if he refuses, he will be denied certain rights. Rabbi Wosner confirms that
based on these circumstances, the Husband was told that he cannot be allowed to
give a
get
under Jewish law.

[
29
]

The second letter is dated April 11, 2021 and is
signed by Rabbi S.A. Indig. Rabbi Indig indicates that he and his colleagues
conducted an investigation and concluded that the Husband is being threatened
and that if he does not give the
get,
proceedings will be taken against
him “with the Youth protection and Criminal etc.”Rabbi Indig indicates that he
learned of these threats through a “witness” who he does not identify. Rabbi
Indig concludes by indicating that a
get
cannot be given through
pressure and that if the Husband gives the
get
under such circumstances,
it will be considered void.

[
30
]

The letters were not filed as expert reports and
the Husband did not seek to present them as such. Consequently, the opinions
that they contain in regards to religious law will not be considered.
[10]

[
31
]

Furthermore, the Court gives no probative weight
to the facts contained in the two letters that go beyond what the Husband
attests to in his sworn declaration. Neither Rabbi Wosner nor Rabbi Indig were
called to testify, their statements were not given under oath and the sources
of their information, apart from the Husband himself, are not identified.

[
32
]

The Husband argues that his refusal to give the
get

is based on a genuine ground of a religious nature. In his view, he cannot
freely give his consent to the
get
so long as there exists a conflict of
any kind with the Wife. According to him, unless all issues are resolved,
including the litigation, his consent cannot be freely given and no
get
would
be valid without it.

[
33
]

The Husband’s position raises a number of
questions as to what constitutes a refusal based on a genuine religious ground.

[
34
]

The Court has no difficulty accepting the
Husband’s position that in order to be valid under Jewish law, a
get

must be given freely. The same concept is part of the
Civil Code of Quebec
,
which provides that consent must be “free and enlightened”.
[11]
However, there is a
considerable difference between the notion that consent to give the
get

must be freely given and the Husband’s position that such consent can never be
freely given so long as there remains a conflict with the spouse. It is unclear
whether the Husband’s expansive view of the concept of consent is an accepted
part of Jewish law or simply his view.
[12]

[
35
]

Furthermore, is the Husband expressing a
religious ground for refusing to give the
get
or merely stating that he
cannot be compelled to decide? Given the context, it stands to reason that the Husband
should be required to go beyond stating that he is not obliged to give the
get

and actually explain why he refuses to give it.

[
36
]

As for the Husband’s willingness to attend a
beth
din,
the Court questions if he can really be prepared to participate in
that process with a view to resolving all the issues associated with his marriage,
which presumably includes the
get
, and still hold a genuine belief that
he cannot give the
get
while any form of conflict exists with the Wife.

[
37
]

In the Court’s view it is not necessary to
answer any of these questions to decide the issue. For the following reasons,
even if the Husband’s refusal to provide the
get
is based on a genuine
ground of a religious nature, the Court would still exercise its powers under
s. 21.1(3) of the Act and grant the Application.

[
38
]

According to
s. 21.1(4)
of the
Act
, a court may
refuse to exercise its powers under s. 21.1 (3) if it is satisfied that a
genuine religious or conscientious justification for refusing to give the
get

has been established; it is certainly not required to do so. Clearly, Parliament
did not intend for such a justification to bind the Court.

[
39
]

Section 21.1
of the
Act
is intended to prevent a
spouse from using the refusal to consent to religious remarriage as leverage to
extract concessions in the context of a civil divorce.
[13]
The position put forward by
the Husband turns this intention on its head. In essence, he argues that the
civil divorce proceedings put pressure on him to agree to give the
get
. As
long as those proceedings remain, he claims to be unable to freely consent.

[
40
]

The issue the Husband raises is not unique to
his particular situation. If it applies to him, it applies to any Jewish spouse
who refuses to give the
get
and would effectively undermine the purpose
of
s. 21.1
of the
Act
.

[
41
]

The discretion not to apply the sanctions
provided for in
s. 21.1 (3)
of the
Act
should be exercised carefully, keeping
in mind Parliament’s objective in adopting
s. 21.1
. To endorse a position that
would render that provision ineffective, which is what the Husband is asking
the Court to do, would not be an appropriate or judicious exercise of that
discretion.

[
42
]

Accordingly, whether or not the Husband’s
position amounts to a genuine religious justification to refuse to give the
get
,
the Court will exercise its powers under s. 21.1 (3) of the Act and will grant
the Application.

REMAINING
ISSUES

[
43
]

The Husband submits that if the Court chooses to
grant the Application, it should only do so in regards to the Divorce file and
not the 04 file.

[
44
]

The Wife acknowledges that the proceedings in
the 04 file are not taken under the
Act
but argues that, under the
circumstances, the Court can and should exercise its discretion to extend its
order to those proceedings.

[
45
]

The Court does not agree that it has the power
under
s. 21.1
of the
Act
to dismiss or strike out proceedings other than those taken
under the Act. Section 21.1(3) (c) and (d) are explicit: the court may dismiss
any application or strike out proceedings “under this Act”.  Since the proceedings
in the 04 file were not taken under the Act, the Application, which is based
solely on the Act and not on any disposition of the
Code of Civil Procedure
,
cannot extend to them.
[14]

[
46
]

Finally, the Husband submits that the order
sought by the Wife goes further than necessary by asking that he be foreclosed
from pleading. His concern is that he would not be allowed to defend himself in
the context of the Divorce file even if the barrier to religious remarriage
were removed.

[
47
]

Although the Husband’s position has been
rejected by the Court, that does not mean that he has acted in bad faith. Once
he has had the benefit of reading the Court’s reasons, it is possible that he
may remove the barrier to the Wife’s religious remarriage. If that were to
happen, the Court agrees with the Husband that he should not be prevented from
filing proceedings or applications under the
Act
.

[
48
]

Section 21.1(3)
(b) of the
Act
gives the courts
the discretionary power to strike out proceedings and dismiss applications
“subject to any terms that the court considers appropriate”. In granting
applications under
s. 21.1
of the Act, the courts have, on occasion, provided a
delay in which to remove the barrier.
[15]

The Court finds that this is an appropriate response to the Husband’s concerns
in this case.

FOR
THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
49
]

GRANTS
in part,
the Plaintiff’s Motion to Dismiss Defendant’s Proceedings and For an Order of
Foreclosure;

[
50
]

DISMISSES
and
STRIKES
OUT
all applications, pleadings and affidavits filed by the Defendant in
Superior Court file 700-12-051546-208;

[
51
]

AUTHORIZES
the
Defendant to refile any applications, pleadings and affidavits in Superior
Court file 700-12-051546-208, by no later than May 25, 2021, provided that at
the same time, he files an affidavit or sworn declaration, confirming that he
has removed the barrier to the Plaintiff’s religious remarriage that was
identified in the Plaintiff’s affidavit of September 14, 2020;

[
52
]

WITH JUDICIAL COSTS.

pETER KALICHMAN, j.S.C.

Me Eric Kirshner

Goldwater Dubé

Attorneys for the Plaintiff

Me Samy
Staltari

Attorney for the
Defendant

In this respect, it is important to point out the Husband is not
alleging that his freedom of religion is infringed under the
Quebec Charter of
Human Rights and Freedoms
or the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.
Consequently, it is far from clear that the expansive view of freedom of
religion endorsed by the Supreme Court in
Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem
,

2004 SCC 47 (CanLII)
, [2004] 2 SCR 551, is applicable.

[13]

9
.

In
Droit de la famille – 151954
,
2015 QCCS 3717
, Justice
Mandeville, faced with a similar application, suspended proceedings in a
related file but did not dismiss them. No request to
suspend was made here.

[15]

Droit de la famille 3558 -
[
2000] R.D.F.
268 (C.S.), p. 270
; A.D. c. J.P.,
2004 CanLII 9414
(C.S.), René Hurtubise,
J.C.S., p. 8;

-

. See also Droit de la famille – 112747,

35
, in
which the Court of Appeal held that in the particular circumstances of that
case, the motions judge should have considered imposing conditions such as an
ultimate delay in which to remove the barrier to religious remarriage.
